articles.title: From true contenders to tankers, ranking all 32 NFL teams by tiers entering the season
articles.summary: Which of the four tiers — True contenders, If everything breaks right..., Work to Do or Tankers — did your team land in?
articles.body:
Power rankings aren't the only way we can sort teams prior to the 2026 NFL season.

As any fantasy footballer worth their salt will tell you, linear rankings can tell you only so much. There might be a huge gap between the fourth and fifth best quarterbacks, or the seventh and eighth running backs, even if their names are next to each other on a list.

The same is true with measuring NFL teams' relative talent; there are dropoffs at different junctures. Instead, we're employing a tiered system indicating where teams are now based on talent, expectations and concerns. It's not a perfect system, but it's an interesting way to look at the league's big picture and see how the clubs size up, apples to apples.

Grouping teams into one of four categories doesn't mean that the top two are guaranteed a playoff run, or that the bottom two should plan on a long season — just ask the Seahawks and Patriots, two big climbers a year ago.

This is also not to say that every team within each category is on even footing. Rather, they're all lumped together with similar caliber strengths, weaknesses and unknowns.

Here's how we see the league stacking up prior to Week 1:

This tier is reserved for the best of the best. We're not talking unflawed teams here, but they're the ones with the most overall firepower to make deep playoff runs and potentially compete for a Super Bowl.

The Rams and Seahawks could be in their own tier, honestly, but that feels too elitist for a league that consistently churns over the top and bottom tiers on a nearly annual basis. Still, we're talking about the team that blowtorched the offseason — and which was just a hair behind the Seahawks a year ago — and the actual Super Bowl champs. And for the record, anyone sleeping on Seattle does so at their own risk. They're still in terrific shape for a title defense.

The Bills and Ravens took steps backward last season but still possess the QB firepower and all-around strength, even with coaching changes, to merit a spot here. The Eagles and Broncos might not have as much offensive heft, but their defenses and overall roster balance earn them rightful spots here.

The final two teams, the 49ers and Patriots, might not belong here on everyone's lists. But the 49ers won a road playoff game in the NFL's toughest division, despite being ravaged by injuries, and New England rode Drake Maye all the way to the Super Bowl. Flawed or not, the Patriots deserve respect and have a reasonable path back to the playoffs.

This next tier probably isn't that far below the upper group, but there are either more questions about these teams' stability or they possess one significant flaw that holds them back a bit.

Three of the four NFC North teams reside here, making up what might be the league's strongest division top to bottom. The Bears and Lions have the offensive firepower to be Super Bowl entrants, but can their defenses hold teams enough? The Packers might be slightly more balanced overall, but their defensive questions could linger until Micah Parsons' return.

The Texans and Chargers have similar makeups: strong to elite defenses, matched with offenses that don't always rise to the occasion on the biggest stages, making this a critical season for C.J. Stroud and Justin Herbert.

The Bengals and Cowboys each could be elite teams this season. Few are worried about them scoring, and all it might take to contend at high levels is moderate improvement defensively. Both clubs have pumped in resources on that side of the ball, so the potential is there.

The Chiefs reasonably could belong in the elite category, but last season's collapse — playing a tier below this down the stretch — and the uncertainty after Patrick Mahomes' ACL injury are reasonable reasons for pause. The Jaguars might be the toughest to slot of this group, coming off a nine-win improvement, but they were a very balanced team and deserve proper respect for that.

Truthfully, the Seahawks and Patriots likely would have begun last season in this category, so it's a reminder that there are no finished products entering Week 1 and no final judgements embossed on anyone. These teams all have elements that could result in contending seasons, but there are at least a few things with each that keep a lid on their potential until further notice.

The Bucs, Steelers, Vikings and Colts all had stretches last season where they were competent to very good contenders with some actual clout, but they all had incomplete seasons. With good health and more consistent quarterback play, each of them are capable of rising up the ranks.

The remaining teams in this tier have redeemable qualities and could outperform expectations. Can the Saints, Panthers or Falcons steal the South? All reasonable possibilities. Are the Giants or Commanders due for bounce-back seasons with better QB health and more defensive efficiency? Perhaps, with the right development and luck.

Atlanta's shaky preseason and big questions had me wondering whether the Falcons belonged here or one slot lower, but their elite skill-position talent was enough for them to hold steady here.

Of course no one is suggesting these teams are tanking on purpose. This is a tough category to find your squad residing in, but it's not purgatory either. It wouldn't be impossible for one of these teams to surprise this season.

The Raiders have upgraded at quarterback and are armed with young talent. There's excitement surrounding the Titans if Cam Ward takes a step up. The Jets had a strong draft class and got some key players back from injury.

The Browns have stacked two impressive draft classes together and might only need QB and OL stability to compete. The Cardinals and Dolphins are not devoid of talent, either.

It's just that these teams likely have the most hurdles to clear and the most big-picture questions surrounding them. Some are likely candidates for the QB derby in next year's draft, and you can't definitively say any of them are completely set at the position, which gives an indication of where they stand at the sport's most important spot.

articles.title: “Prepared 500 servings for 125 local families”: Patrick and Brittany Mahomes’ 15 and the Mahomies team up with Pete’s Garden, Shelter KC and FARE for Kansas City community impact
articles.summary: NFL News: Patrick and Brittany Mahomes’ charitable work through their 15 and the Mahomies foundation has addressed various needs across the Kansas City communit.
articles.body: Patrick and Brittany Mahomes’ charitable work through their 15 and the Mahomies foundation has addressed various needs across the Kansas City community, from food insecurity to food allergy education.Through separate partnerships with Pete’s Garden, Shelter KC, and Food Allergy Research & Education [FARE], the foundation has wholeheartedly supported families with meals, community resources, and practical, reliable information designed to make day-to-day life safer, better, and more manageable.The initiatives emphasize that access to food involves much more than putting a meal on the table. For some families, the challenge is food insecurity. For others, specifically those managing food allergies, navigating meals safely can require valuable education, public awareness, and trustworthy support.Patrick and Brittany Mahomes’ 15 and the Mahomies foundation supports students while providing hundreds of meal servingsIn partnership with Pete’s Garden, the 15 and the Mahomies foundation supported a heartfelt initiative that brought culinary education and community service together back in April 2025.At Manual Career Technical Center in the Kansas City Public School District, culinary students sincerely prepared 500 servings of Lentil Ragu over Pasta for approximately 125 local families served by Boys & Girls Clubs of Greater Kansas City.“When students realize they can cook a meal that feeds a community, something changes,” said Tamara Weber, Founder and Executive Director of Pete’s Garden. “By equipping educators with the tools and resources to lead impactful service projects, we’re building a movement of young leaders who understand the power of food to create change.”The insightful effort was part of Pete’s Garden’s Kids Feeding Kids program, which provides high school students with real-world, hands-on experience planning, preparing, and packaging family-sized meals.The service-learning opportunity also familiarizes students with serious issues surrounding food insecurity and food access within their own communities.The sagacious collaboration generated a dual impact: families received prepared meals, while young culinary students grasped real-world experience and a rare opportunity to use their developing skills in service of others.“Sitting down as a family to a healthy and wholesome meal is something Brittany and I really value,” said Patrick Mahomes.“But too many Kansas City families are struggling to get a wholesome dinner on the table. We are proud to support Kids Feeding Kids and help make mealtime easier for these families while also engaging students in a meaningful community service experience.”Patrick and Brittany Mahomes’ Thanksgiving partnership with Shelter KCFor 75 years, Shelter KC has been a haven for Kansas City’s homeless men and women. In November 2024, Patrick and Brittany Mahomes’ 15 and the Mahomies foundation worked with them to support Kansas City families dealing with hardship during the holiday season.The foundation made a $15,000 donation to support Shelter KC’s annual Thanksgiving Family Feast.The contribution was wholeheartedly intended to provide Thanksgiving dinners for over 200 Kansas City families in need. Shelter KC and foundation volunteers were scheduled to prepare meal boxes and help create a celebration day centered on food preparation, building connection, and community service.The Thanksgiving partnership mirrored the foundation’s comprehensive commitment to supporting children and families through initiatives concentrated on health, wellness, and community resources, while also helping extend Shelter KC’s reach during the festive time of year. When nobody deserves to be sad or in need of wholesome food.“We are incredibly grateful to 15 and the Mahomies foundation for this support,” said Shelter KC Executive Director Eric Burger.“Their partnership is an inspiring reminder that we are all part of the same community, responsible for lifting one another up. This donation ensures that families who may be struggling this holiday season will have a Thanksgiving meal to enjoy together, and a renewed sense of hope for the future.”Brittany Mahomes brings food allergy education to Kansas City familiesFood-related support has also become a crucial portion of the foundation’s work through its partnership with FARE [Food Allergy Research & Education]. The joint initiative, known as “15 and FARE,” was established to expand food allergy education, support, and resources throughout the Kansas City area.On July 18, 2026, from 1 to 4 PM, “15 and FARE” hosted a free Back-to-School event at the Kansas City Public Library’s Plaza Branch for Kansas City-area families managing food allergies. The afternoon event included a Top 9 allergen-free school lunch demonstration, an Ask-the-Expert panel, a kids’ fun zone, and other health resources.The free open-to-the-public event was designed to help families prepare for the new school year while addressing questions that can arise when children with food allergies return to cafeteria lunches, classroom activities, field trips, and extracurricular programs where their parents or caregivers are not by their side.“As a food allergy mom myself, I know how important it is for families to feel prepared and supported, especially during back-to-school season,” said Brittany Mahomes, food allergy advocate and 15 and the Mahomies co-founder.“For parents managing food allergies, having access to trusted resources and a strong community can make all the difference. 15 and the Mahomies is proud to partner with FARE to bring Kansas City families together for a day of learning, connection, and fun.”Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Patrick Mahomes faces major Chiefs problem as injuries to Rashee Rice and Xavier Worthy expose receiving corps concerns
articles.summary: NFL News: Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs have a concern before their 2026 season opener: the wide receiver room. CBS Sports’ Jared Dubin ranked Kans.
articles.body: Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs have a concern before their 2026 season opener: the wide receiver room. CBS Sports’ Jared Dubin ranked Kansas City 29th among all 32 NFL teams at the position, pointing to injury concerns around Rashee Rice and Xavier Worthy. The Chiefs face the Denver Broncos on September 14, while Mahomes is expected to start after his knee surgery.Patrick Mahomes faces concern as Chiefs wide receivers rank 29thDubin’s ranking puts the spotlight on a group that has not had much stability. “With Rashee Rice still looking hobbled after rehabbing his knee injury in jail and Xavier Worthy again banged up in camp, the Chiefs might be counting on training-camp star Cyrus Allen to be a real factor, rather than a mere curiosity. That’s a dangerous game to play,” Dubin wrote for CBS Sports.Kansas City kept six wide receivers on its initial 53-man roster: Rice, Worthy, Tyquan Thornton, Jalen Royals, Nikko Remigio and Cyrus Allen. That leaves less room for proven depth if one of the main targets cannot play or is limited. The Chiefs had seven receivers in 2023 and 2024 and eight in 2025.Worthy enters the season with a chance to become a bigger part of the offense. He caught 42 passes for 532 yards and one touchdown last season despite playing through injuries. ESPN’s Dan Graziano has also pointed out that Kansas City had bigger plans for Worthy last year before a shoulder injury suffered on the third play of the season limited what the team could ask him to do.Xavier Worthy gives Patrick Mahomes a positive updateWorthy gave the Chiefs a reason to feel better on Wednesday. Speaking to reporters, he said he and Mahomes have spent the offseason working on their timing. “Me and Pat, we’ve kind of been working this offseason and obviously the timing and stuff you need to work on. . . . I feel like when it’s time to play, we’ll all be ready,” Worthy said, via NBC Sports.That connection could matter because Denver is the first test. The bigger news is that Mahomes appears ready to return. The Associated Press reported Wednesday that he has worked with the first team in camp after December surgery to repair torn ligaments in his left knee.Doctors had initially suggested October as a possible return, but Mahomes moved faster than expected. He did not play during the preseason, but that was planned. Chiefs coach Andy Reid said Wednesday, “He’s going to keep practicing just like he’s been doing,” while explaining that the team’s work before the opener will include more one-on-one practice.There is still an issue in front of him. Left tackle Josh Simmons remained out Wednesday with a back injury, while guard Trey Smith has been dealing with a hip injury. Kansas City has added depth on the line, but Mahomes could enter Week 1 with questions around both his protection and his receivers.For now, the Chiefs have a quarterback who appears on track to play and a receiving group that must prove the 29th-place ranking wrong.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Dianna Russini's relationship with Mike Vrabel was 'in clear violation' of standards, The Athletic review says
articles.summary: The Athletic's standards review found Dianna Russini's relationship with Mike Vrabel violated company policy, raising questions about trust and disclosure.
articles.body: The Athletic has released a long-awaited standards review about former reporter Dianna Russini's relationship with New England Patriots coach Mike Vrabel and it paints the media entity as something of a trusting victim of a reporter who hid truth from her employer. The report does not attempt to conclude whether Russini had a romantic or physical relationship with Vrabel that helped her reporting through the years. But the report, authored by The Athletic's editorial director for standards and quality Mike Semel, ultimately decided that the company was uncomfortable with the relationship Russini had with Vrabel. THE ATHLETIC EXECUTIVE EDITOR ADMITS KEY MISTAKE MADE IN IN HANDLING OF DIANNA RUSSINI CONTROVERSY: REPORT "Russini’s relationship with Vrabel was in clear violation of The Athletic’s standards," the report reads. "Regardless of whether the relationship was romantic, it was a breach and should have been disclosed." Semel believes Russini didn't use her platform to promote Vrabel. But he does not delve into the obvious possibility that the reporter used the relationship to help her own career. "I’ve not found a clear link to conclude that Russini used her platform to help promote Vrabel or help his teams during her time at The Athletic," Semel writes. "That said, there are examples of Russini writing glowingly of Vrabel that in hindsight are awkward or even uncomfortable." And let's be clear: The Athletic should be "uncomfortable" with Russini covering Vrabel "glowingly" because it raises an unspoken possibility of a quid pro quo exchange between the journalist and the coach that might help her work product The Athletic report cited only one story by Russini that "likely would not have happened were it not for the connection between Russini and Vrabel." The Athletic said its methodology in doing this investigation was extensive. It ... A source familiar with the report told OutKick that Russini did not speak with Semel for this report nor was her phone available for inspection by The Athletic. The report states that on April 7, 2026, Russini contacted executives at The Athletic and The New York Times Company to tell them of an impending Page Six article that would suggest a romantic relationship between her and Vrabel. She told her bosses the story would include photographs of the pair together, taken at a Sedona, Arizona resort. Russini apparently acknowledged a close relationship with Vrabel at that time, "but stressed that it was strictly professional," the report states. Page Six eventually published photos of Russini and Vrabel on the roof of a bungalow holding hands and embracing. It also published photos of the pair at a pool and at a hot tub together. CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM It should be noted that The Athletic did not contact Vrabel in authoring this report. It did, however, speak with Russini's friends and colleagues within the company. The report does not specify if The Athletic asked Russini to provide exculpatory evidence that would alleviate concerns the company might have about a relationship it found in violation of its standards. And ultimately, The Athletic report makes it clear that Russini lost trust within the company because of the manner she handled the release of the New York Post's information. "[W]hen first confronted with the photos by The New York Post," Semel explains, "Russini waited two days before telling her editors and managers. She then told a story to explain the photos that did not align with facts, raising issues of trust." Vrabel has suffered no professional discipline from this episode, neither from the NFL nor the Patriots. Russini resigned her post from The Athletic months ago and even deleted her social media presence. She has not commented publicly about the issue beyond social media — at least not yet. FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

articles.title: Athletic’s review of former NFL reporter Dianna Russini concludes she didn’t comply with standards
articles.summary: The report drew no conclusions about the nature of Russini’s relationship with Vrabel, who said he took accountability for his actions without addressing pho...
articles.body:
An investigation by The Athletic has concluded that former NFL reporter Dianna Russini violated the company's standards because of her relationship with New England Patriots coach Mike Vrabel that led to her resignation in April.

The report drew no conclusions about the nature of Russini's relationship with Vrabel, who said he took accountability for his actions without addressing photos released of the coach and the reporter at a resort in Arizona. He stepped away from the team on the third day of the NFL draft to begin counseling and returned soon afterward.

"We neither completed an investigation nor reached any conclusion about the nature of the full relationship between Vrabel and Russini, but the totality of the public photographs are enough to conclude a violation of company policy," the report said.

Steven Ginsberg, executive editor at The Athletic, a New York Times-owned sports outlet, addressed the report in a message to employees Thursday.

"We undertook this review to ensure the integrity of our journalism and to maintain the trust our audience places in us. Nothing is more important than our credibility," Ginsberg wrote.

Mike Semel, editorial director for standards and quality at The Athletic, conducted the review of Russini's work, examining 903 stories, 204 episodes of her podcast and 77 videos.

"The review found that the vast majority of Dianna's stories were unrelated to Vrabel, and most of those that mentioned him did not raise concerns," Ginsberg told the staff. "We have, however, added editor's notes to four stories — one written and three videos — that did not meet our standards."

The photos of Vrabel and Russini were taken in Sedona, Arizona, before the annual NFL meetings that began in Phoenix on March 29, according to the New York Post. Vrabel and Russini are both married. The NFL did not investigate Vrabel's actions.

Vrabel led the Patriots to the Super Bowl in February, where they lost to Seattle. He was the AP NFL Coach of the Year in his first season in New England, finishing 63 points ahead of Jacksonville's Liam Coen.

Russini told the AP on Thursday that she stands by what she wrote in her resignation letter in April.

"I have covered the NFL with professionalism and dedication throughout my career, and I stand behind every story I have ever published. When the Page Six item first appeared, The Athletic supported me unequivocally, expressed confidence in my work and pride in my journalism. For that I am grateful. In the days that followed, unfortunately, commentators in various media have engaged in self-feeding speculation that is simply unmoored from the facts," Russini said then, adding she was stepping away "not because I accept the narrative that has been constructed around this episode, but because I refuse to lend it further oxygen or to let it define me or my career."

articles.title: 49ers, Rams hoping big-name players will be healthy enough to play in Australia matchup
articles.summary: Nick Bosa and George Kittle are among the players recovering from injuries who hope to be on the field in Week 1.
articles.body:
The San Francisco 49ers and Los Angeles Rams will open their seasons next Thursday in an historic matchup from Melbourne, Australia.

While the 49ers have already begun their trek down under, the Rams will not be arriving until a day before the game , which kicks off on Friday, Sept. 11, at 11:35 a.m local time.

As both teams prepare for Week 1, there are several lingering injury storylines to track. A number of key players are working their way toward being ready to play, but a few have yet to get a green light.

After tearing his Achilles in January, the tight end is trending in a positive direction as far as playing next week. Kittle practiced this week and, according to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport , there is an "optimistic sense" of the 32-year-old being available against the Rams. Like Nick Bosa, he was on the plane to Australia with the team on Wednesday.

The defensive end practiced fully for the first time in training camp on Wednesday, nearly a year after tearing his right ACL. He told reporters that he "felt great" and said the progress he is making is "very encouraging." As far as playing Week 1, he did not say anything definitive, but sounded like he was expecting to be out there next Friday (Thursday in the U.S.). Teams doctors will have the final say, of course.

"It was a long road," Bosa told reporters via ESPN.com . "There's some stuff I dealt with, with that patella tendon, and then I kind of ramped it a little too fast with the football stuff a month ago or whatever it was. And that kind of told me to back off. I've just been trying to get it as strong and myself as confident as I can to where I could rip the Band-Aid off and go to team stuff today."

The veteran receiver has been out for most of training camp with an adductor injury. He returned to practice this week. As with Kittle, there is optimism that the offseason signing will be ready to go next Thursday.

"We've got some solid work throughout the offseason," said 49ers general manager John Lynch on Tuesday. "He ran into a little hiccup with his adductor, but he's working really well to the side, and hope to get him back here early next week. And if all goes well, he'll be suiting up and making plays for us, and that's all the guy's done throughout his career."

The goal is Week 1 for the reigning NFL Defensive Player of the Year and current No. 1 player in the league . He has dealt with lower body soreness, and most recently knee swelling, that's kept him away from the field. Rams head coach Sean McVay said this week that Garrett is "making good progress" and the "goal all along has been [playing in] Australia."

The Rams receiver has been bothered by psoas soreness since mid-August, but made his return to practice on Sunday. The team has no concern moving forward and he is expected to be involved next week against the 49ers.

articles.title: From test cricket marathons to the NFL: Melbourne’s MCG readies for Rams-49ers
articles.summary: A debut Down Under has been a long time coming for the NFL.  It's fitting, too, that the Los Angeles Rams and the San Francisco 49ers will be playing their s...
articles.body:
BRISBANE, Australia (AP) — A debut Down Under has been a long time coming for the NFL . It's a good thing Aussies revel in the long game.

It's fitting, too, that the Los Angeles Rams and the San Francisco 49ers will be playing their season-opening game next week at the Melbourne Cricket Ground — known locally as the MCG or, more commonly, just as The G.

At 100,000 capacity, it's a big ground for a big occasion in a city that loves hosting big events. It's where for almost 150 years Australia has been playing test cricket matches, which can run across five days yet still finish without a winner, and it's the home of Australian rules football.

It has hosted the Olympics, Cricket World Cup finals, some of Taylor Swift's biggest shows and even a Papal mass.

Established in 1853, The G has developed a revered place in Australian sports and cultural life. Australia's premier venue will host the first of the NFL's nine international games this season .

The NFL ran a bid process across multiple Australian states for the debut Down Under and it was the MCG, being so cherished and so close to downtown, that sealed it. Along with Melbourne's success delivering high-profile events including the Australian Open — the season-opening tennis major at the adjoining Melbourne Park — and the Australian F1 Grand Prix .

"Melbourne as a city really stood out, having a huge stadium of that size, that caliber, that historical nature, in the middle of the city," Charlotte Offord, GM for NFL Australia/New Zealand, told The Associated Press. "It just felt like a bit of a no-brainer."

A cathedral, a colosseum ... it's not just cricket

Former Prime Minister John Howard, a self-described cricket tragic, once characterized the MCG as a place of worship.

In a 1996 speech at The G, Howard recounted how he'd mentioned to the Catholic archbishop that after visiting St. Patrick's Cathedral, "I was going to one of the spiritual centers, the true temporal shrine and sporting shrine, not only of Melbourne but also of Australia."

"Without any doubt the Melbourne Cricket Ground is the greatest sporting arena in our nation, and I think probably without comparison anywhere in the world."

It helps that Melburnians are renowned for a love of sport. It can create the kind of atmosphere at The G that cricket icon Dennis Lillee, the mustachioed and hairy chested fast bowler of the 1970s and 80s, compared with the ancient arena in Rome.

"To me the MCG is the people's ground,'' Lillee told Fox Sports before the Boxing Day test in 2014. It's not about the facilities, "It's the people. Even though the wicket was flat and the ball was old and dead, the crowd lifted you. They would go to watch ant racing. But for crowd involvement as an arena, a coliseum, the MCG was my favorite.''

It was a theme the late, great Shane Warne embraced, too. So much so that a big part of the homegrown cricket star's state memorial service was staged at the stadium in 2022 and a stand was renamed in his honor.

A week and many time zones away from that famous kiss with Travis Kelce after the Chiefs beat the 49ers in the 2024 Super Bowl, Swift told the crowd after three sold-out shows on her Eras tour at the MCG: "Melbourne, you are the love of my life. I cannot believe you, what you have done."

"Ninety-six thousand people the first night, 96,000 people the second night, 96,000 people tonight," she said. "All of that, those are all the biggest shows I've ever played on a tour and you did it three times!"

Swift's influence has helped grow the popularity of American football in Australia . Girls and young women account for a big proportion of the NFL's growing fanbase in Australia.

"I'd put that down to, one, flag football and girls playing," Offord said. "I'd also put it down to the Taylor Swift effect. We don't hide behind that at all — she has done great things for the league in terms of her ability to bring a new demographic of people into the fold."

The G has been home to Australian rules football since 1859, and has a pride of place in cricket history. Australia hosted England there in the very first official cricket test in 1877 — the forerunner to the Ashes contests between the two countries — and the first one-day international in 1971. The 1992 and 2015 World Cup finals were decided here.

It was the main stadium for the 1956 Olympics and the 2006 Commonwealth Games.

The MCG hosted baseball as early as 1888. In 1914, the New York Giants and Chicago White Sox played there.

While high-profile soccer, rugby union, rugby league and Gaelic football games have been contested at the G, American football's previous exposure to the venue has been limited. A 1908 game featuring teams from a visiting U.S. Navy fleet is one example.

As well as sports and concerts, the G has hosted the armed forces. In World War II, it housed a U.S. Army Air Forces depot called Camp Murphy, a regiment of the U.S. Marine Corps in 1943 and Royal Australian Air Force personnel.

American evangelist Billy Graham pulled the biggest crowd ever at the G — more than 130,000 in 1959. The biggest attendance for an Australian rules match is a touch under 122,000. By the mid-90s annual attendances for events at the MCG exceeded 3.5 million. The record aggregate crowd for a cricket match is 373,691 — across five days of the Ashes test in 2024.

Only Ed Sheeran has pulled a bigger concert crowd than Swift — his 107,243 in 2023 is the MCG record.

Situated in Yarra Park, the MCG is a 15-minute walk along the river to the city center and easily accessible by trams and trains.

The capacity is now 100,024, including 95,000 seated. The playing arena is oval shaped and is 174-meters (190 yards) at its longest length and 149 meters (163 yards) at his widest width. The rectangular NFL field will easily fit within the arena, but organizers say there won't be too much "dead space."

"We obviously have a lot of extra players that come with our game, (plus) cheerleaders, entertainment, equipment," Offord said. "You'll be surprised at (how little) space is actually left."

Will Bryce, head of the NFL's youth academy in Australia, said the MCG has an "aura you can just feel when you step in."

"It's going to be an incredible atmosphere," he said. "It's going to be a great collaboration between the NFL and everyone else involved."

articles.title: Grading Michael Wilson's $75 million extension to uplift Cardinals offense
articles.summary: Is Wilson ready to be a true WR1? Or was his 2025 breakthrough a product of circumstance that can't be duplicated?
articles.body:
The Arizona Cardinals hoped 2025 would be the year Marvin Harrison Jr. fulfilled his promise as a former top five draft pick. It was a different young wide receiver who rose up instead.

Wilson caught fire late in his third year as a pro. After a modest start, he put up a 119-catch, 1,600-yard, 13-touchdown full season pace after Week 11 for a Cardinals team in desperate need of playmakers. He finished the year with more than 1,000 receiving yards. While a good chunk of that can be attributed to a bad team trailing often and throwing the ball more than any other NFL team, it was still encouraging.

On Thursday, Arizona rewarded his rise. The Cardinals reportedly signed the 26-year-old wideout to a three-year, $75 million contract extension with $47 million guaranteed. It's a deal that will keep him in Glendale to see through another wave of his team's attempt to find a franchise quarterback. But was it the right move?

The deal: Arizona Cardinals sign WR Michael Wilson to a three-year, $75 million contract extension with $47 million guaranteed

Wilson was a pleasant complementary piece in 2023 and 2024. He looked to be locked into a similar role in 2025, but the transition from Kyler Murray to Jacoby Brissett helped spark a prolific finish to his third season.

Was some of that a Marqise Lee/ Jacksonville Jaguars "we're trailing and gotta throw the hell out of the ball in the second half" type opportunity? Certainly! But Wilson's underlying numbers suggest this is sustainable (and, also, Lee was pretty useful in 2017 when Jacksonville probably should have made it to the Super Bowl).

Despite playing with subpar quarterbacks, Wilson has recorded a catch rate over expected (CROE) of at least plus-4.5 percent in each of his seasons as a pro. He's had a positive yards after catch over expected (YACOE) in all of those years as well. He was a positive force on all three levels downfield, but made his biggest impact as an intermediate, chain-moving resource 10-19 yards downfield (plus-8.3 percent CROE, 9.8 yards per target and a ton of contested, Jacoby Brissett-bailing catches).

That's proof he can be an uplifting force for a flawed quarterback. And if there's one thing the Cardinals have lots of, it's flawed QBs. He can be the huckleberry for Brissett, Gardner Minshew II or Carson Beck this season. He can be the huckleberry of whomever the team drafts near the top of the first round in 2027.

He'll also help draw focus away from Harrison. The tantalizing prospect was largely inactive as Wilson rose to WR1 duties, but Harrison's seven target, six-catch performance in Week 13 helped show how these two can help each other. Then again, his average separation per target in games played alongside a surging Wilson was only about 1.6 yards, which suggests he wasn't getting open a ton despite having someone opponents needed to bracket.

So this isn't just a move that shores up the receiving corps; it's a reasonable insurance policy should Harrison never meet his potential. Wilson's $25 million annual average salary ranks only 20th among wide receivers. It's a proper bet, but not a franchise-altering one.

He probably won't average 1,600 yards per season over the life of that deal, but if he's even 85 percent as effective as he was to close out 2025 it will be an underpay. The only concern is the small sample size involved, which knocks this down from an "A" when Arizona could have waited to see if Wilson still had the juice, franchise-tagged him next spring and worked out a (more expensive) deal in the offseason.

articles.title: NFL news, live updates: Raiders name Kirk Cousins as starting QB; George Kittle heads to Australia with 49ers ahead of Week 1 coming off Achilles injury
articles.summary: Follow along with the latest NFL news and injury updates after the preseason wrapped up.
articles.body: With the NFL preseason and Sunday's roster cut deadline in the books, each team's initial 53-man roster has been set. Now, we look toward the 2026 regular season, with practices in full swing leading up to this year's kick-off game between the New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks next Wednesday — a rematch of Super Bowl LX.Headlining the news Wednesday was that Las Vegas Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak named veteran Kirk Cousins the team's starting quarterback for Week 1 against the Miami Dolphins over No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza.On Tuesday, it was reported that Cincinnati Bengals wideout Ja'Marr Chase will be limited in practices this week after hyperextending his knee last week. Tee Higgins is also limited with a heel contusion, though head coach Zach Taylor says he expects both of them "will be good at the end of the week."Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Football league for the 2026 NFL seasonAlso, Packers running back Josh Jacobs and Broncos LB Jonathon Cooper have been placed on the commissioner's exempt list while the NFL looks into domestic violence allegations against both players. Packers GM Brian Gutekunst said Tuesday that the organization hasn't seen the surveillance video in Jacobs' case and that the Packers will have a contingency plan in place if the three-time Pro Bowler isn't on the field. Recently-signed Indianapolis Colts wideout Keenan Allen also found himself in legal trouble this week after being arrested on charges of driving while intoxicated. GM Chris Ballard offered his support to Allen on Tuesday, saying he'll play in the Colts' season opener, adding, "He's a tremendous human being. Give him some grace."Follow along with Yahoo Sports for the latest NFL news, injury updates and more leading up to Week 1 of the regular season.
